lessons.title: Inspecting racing tack for damage
lessons.html:
Why tack repair matters

Racing tack works hard. It gets wet with sweat, dirty with sand, and pulled hard at speed. Leather dries and cracks, stitching wears, and buckles bend. A rein or girth that breaks at full gallop can cause a fall that injures or kills a horse and jockey. Regular inspection and correct repair are essential safety work.

When to inspect

  • Every time you clean the tack, which should be after every use
  • Before every race and every piece of fast work
  • A full, detailed check once a week

What to look for

PartDamage signs
LeatherCracks when bent, dry and stiff, thin or stretched spots, torn holes
StitchingLoose, rotten, broken or missing stitches, especially at buckles and the bit ends of reins
Buckles and fittingsBent tongues, rust, sharp edges, cracks
Girths and elasticsElastic that does not spring back, frayed webbing
Rubber grips on reinsWorn smooth, peeling, splitting
SaddleBroken tree (the saddle twists or creaks), worn panels, loose stirrup bars

How to check leather

Bend each strap gently in a curve. Good leather bends smoothly. Damaged leather shows small cracks on the surface. Pay extra attention to places where leather folds around a buckle or bit, because they wear fastest.

Decide: repair or replace?

  • Minor: a few loose stitches, a stiff strap that needs oiling, a missing keeper - can often be fixed in the yard.
  • Major: cracked leather on a load-bearing strap, a broken saddle tree, torn girth straps - take out of use, label it, report to the head groom. It may need a saddler or replacement.

When in doubt, take it out of use. Put a tag on damaged items: "Do not use - needs repair". Write it in the tack repair book.

lessons.title: Doing basic tack repairs
lessons.html:
Tools and materials

  • Waxed linen thread and two harness needles
  • Stitching awl or diamond awl for making holes
  • Leather hole punch
  • Sharp leather knife or scissors (cut away from your body)
  • Saddle soap, leather oil or conditioner
  • Spare buckles, keepers and rubber rein grips
  • A stitching clam or clamp to hold the work

Safety with tools

Awls, needles and knives are sharp. Work at a table with good light. Keep your hand behind the point. Store sharp tools in a box after use. Wear safety glasses when punching hard leather.

Re-stitching a seam (saddle stitch)

  1. Clean the leather and remove the old broken thread.
  2. Hold the work in a clamp.
  3. Use the old holes where possible. If needed, make new holes with the awl, evenly spaced.
  4. Thread a needle on each end of one long piece of waxed thread.
  5. Push one needle through the first hole and pull until the thread is even on both sides.
  6. Pass both needles through each hole from opposite sides, crossing in the hole. Pull each stitch tight and even.
  7. Go a few stitches past the damaged area into sound stitching.
  8. Back-stitch two holes to lock, then cut the thread close.

Saddle stitching with two needles is stronger than machine stitching, because if one thread breaks the other still holds.

Other basic repairs

  • Punching a new hole: mark the spot in line with the others, punch cleanly with the right size punch.
  • Replacing a keeper: cut leather to size, stitch the ends, slide on.
  • Replacing rubber grips on reins: follow the head groom's method; usually the grip is slid on and stitched at the ends.
  • Reconditioning dry leather: clean, then oil lightly on the flesh (rough) side, let it soak in.

What you must not repair

Do not try to repair a broken saddle tree, girth straps on the saddle, or a stirrup bar. These need a qualified saddler.

After repair

Pull hard on the repaired part to test it. Show the head groom before the item goes back into use. Record the repair in the tack book.

Key points

  • Inspect tack after every use and before every race.
  • Bend leather to find cracks; check stitching at buckles and bit ends.
  • Tag damaged tack "Do not use" and record it.
  • Saddle stitch with two needles for strength.
  • Saddle trees, girth straps and stirrup bars go to a qualified saddler.
